Jamestown+ by Final Form Games, published by Batterystaple Games, is a standout entry in the top-down shoot ’em up genre that combines old-school arcade action with a fresh and imaginative setting. Set in an alternate 17th-century where British colonial forces have taken to Mars, the game delivers a unique twist on historical fiction with its steampunk-inspired visuals and sci-fi themes. This blend of history and fantasy gives the game a distinct flavor that sets it apart from typical shmups, creating a rich backdrop against which the fast-paced, bullet-hell style combat unfolds.

At its core, Jamestown+ is about precision, timing, and cooperation. The gameplay challenges players to navigate increasingly complex waves of enemies and projectiles while mastering the unique abilities of different ships. Each player’s ship comes equipped with varied weapons and power-ups, allowing for a diversity of playstyles. The inclusion of up to four-player local co-op adds a layer of strategic depth and fun, as teamwork becomes essential for survival, especially at higher difficulties. One of the game’s most notable mechanics is the ability to revive fallen teammates by collecting their souls, which not only encourages players to stay close and support each other but also keeps the tension high during intense moments.

Visually, Jamestown+ is a masterclass in pixel art. The game’s art style pays homage to the golden age of arcade shooters while incorporating detailed and vibrant environments that bring its Martian setting to life. The color palette is rich and varied, with intricate backgrounds and enemy designs that provide visual clarity even amidst the chaotic on-screen action. The animation is smooth, which is crucial in a bullet-hell game where precision dodging is key. Complementing the visuals is an outstanding orchestral soundtrack composed by Francisco Cerda, which perfectly matches the game’s epic and adventurous tone, elevating every firefight and boss encounter with cinematic flair.

Beyond its aesthetic and gameplay merits, Jamestown+ offers a well-balanced challenge that caters to both newcomers and veterans of the genre. The game’s difficulty ramps up steadily, introducing new enemy types, patterns, and environmental hazards that test player skill and adaptability. The campaign is composed of multiple missions, each with unique objectives and escalating stakes, giving a satisfying sense of progression. For players seeking even more challenge, the “Gauntlet” mode pushes endurance and mastery to the limit with its unforgiving series of levels. This depth and replayability ensure that Jamestown+ stays engaging long after the initial playthrough.

While Jamestown+ is generally polished and well-optimized, it has experienced some technical hiccups on certain platforms, including compatibility issues reported on the Steam Deck. These problems, although relatively minor, can disrupt the smoothness of the experience for some players. Additionally, the game’s focus on local multiplayer might limit online play options, which could be a drawback for those looking to play remotely with friends. Nonetheless, these issues do not detract significantly from the overall quality of the game and its appeal.

In conclusion, Jamestown+ is a compelling blend of classic shoot ’em up gameplay with a fresh narrative twist and modern design sensibilities. Its unique setting, cooperative mechanics, and gorgeous pixel art make it a memorable experience that honors the genre’s traditions while pushing creative boundaries. Whether you are a hardcore shmup fan or a player looking for an accessible yet challenging arcade adventure, Jamestown+ offers a rich, rewarding, and visually striking journey through an imaginative Martian frontier. It’s a game that demands skill and teamwork, and in return, delivers exhilarating action and a captivating atmosphere that lingers well after the last bullet has been fired.

Jamestown+ is genuinely one of the best sprite based games I've played yet. They managed to make a widescreen vertical shmup work so well and make it look fantastic, despite the complications most games of this genre have trying to make it work. As a shmup it's really fun, though as a multiplayer experience, I'm not sure since I've been exclusively playing this solo, but I imagine the experience would be just as engaging as it is alone.

The ship variety is making me actually want to experiment with different shot types as it contains more than 12 different ways to shoot your enemies down, though you have to unlock and buy them by progressing the campaign. I personally like it since I have a reason to use the money I earn from each stage clear on the harder difficulties. The main and special shots are still as destructive as I'd like, though there are some that are just outright better than others. There are about 3-4 ships so far that I've unlocked that I clearly spend more time with than others, but maybe it's just preference?

My only gripe with the game is a lack of any clearly visible hurtbox for the player. I find myself getting hit by bullet patterns I can clearly dodge efficiently in other games like Touhou or the many many CAVE games. Those games and many others have either a standard dot that shows your hurtbox, or a clever design detail that acts as a subtle sign that you'll die if you get hit here. Jamestown has nothing like that. The only way you can tell where it's at is when you're selecting your ship before a mission and the game has to point it out to you somewhere on the characters back. It is invisible otherwise, or possibly very unnoticeable. If only they had the spot visible at all times, then the bullet swarms on the harder difficulties would actually make sense. 

Other than that, I highly recommend this game to anyone curious! Either you're already well versed in shmups or you're new and would like to play something that scratches that beautiful sprite work itch that makes you gawk at the visuals. If you're interested, it's worth it!

C’est du shmup typé « bullet hell » avec de supers beaux graphismes pixel-art et un délire scénaristique assez marrant portant une ambiance singulière et sympa (les conquistador ne colonisent pas l’Amérique, mais Mars).

Après j’ai trouvé ça « pas si fou » et même parfois bêtement obtus, dans sa fascination pour le no hit (on est détruit par n’importe quel impact ; même si on a qqs vies et même qqs crédits … qui ne se distinguent en rien d’ailleurs ; si ce n’est que l’écran de crédit offre le bon vieux compte-à-rebours pour accepter le crédit … mais en fait pas moyen de le « refuser », l’artificialité du truc devenant un peu bêtat, mais bon). Le jeu offrant aussi plusieurs niveaux de difficulté … mais nous imposant à l’augmenter pour progresser dans l’aventure (les niveaux perdant au fur et à mesure les options de difficultés plus basses, avec derniers niveaux jouables uniquement en difficile … pas compris l’idée vue que les niveaux peuvent (doivent, même, logiquement) être de plus en plus corsés au fur et à mesure de la progression à niveau de difficulté constant … donc bon … encore un truc bizaroïde mais bref …).

Après je suis surement pas bon juge parce que j’ai toujours énormément de mal à me faire aux hitbox qui n’ocupent qu’une partie du sprite dessiné à l’écran (et c’est pas une option de bien l’intégrer car on ne peut pas, au bout d’un moment, faire l’économie des esquives « au poil de cul » au milieu de rideaux de boulettes, en usant finement des limites de cette hitbox et pas du sprite dessiné) ; en plus un peu de mal, pour naviguer finement (chose encore indispensable) avec le déplacement à vitesse unique ne jouant pas avec la progressivité que permet le stick analogique ; mieux vaut finalement recourir à la croix directionnelle finalement pour un meilleur feeling et réactivité sur ce point, mais on perd alors les directions libres (contraintes dès lors à des horizontales / verticales ou diagonales à 45° strictes) …).

A cela s’ajoute une mécanique clé qui veut qu’en ramassant des collectables abandonnés par les ennemis détruits on charge une barre d’énergie qui permet, une fois pleine, d’activer un bouclier qui immunise un instant et fait passer en mode de dégats augmentés, qu’on peut maintenir en continuant d’accumuler de l’énergie. Le truc un peu foireux je trouve, bah c’est que le bouclier fugace est bien utile pour se sauver de certaines situations critiques, mais qu’en même temps il est assez crucial d’être autant que possible en mode « tir augmenté » (et de s’y maintenir) car détruire plus rapidement les ennemis est assez crucial pour ne pas se faire submerger ; mais comme les deux mécaniques sont liées, on peut être tenté de garder sa barre pleine pour pouvoir déclencher le bouclier en cas de besoin ; mais on reste alors en mode « tir de base » ce qui rend la gestion des ennemis autrement plus délicate … bref, je trouve cette mécanique plus foireuse et frustrante qu’intéressante … (à noter pour être tout à fait précis qu’on peut aussi désactiver le mode « tir augmenté » ce qui réactive un bouclier plus fugace, mais cela se double du blocage à zéro de la barre d’énergie pendant un certain temps, empêchant des enchainements astucieux, bref, implémenté de la sorte ça rajoute plus au caractère bancal de la mécanique que ça ne l’enrichie je trouve …)

Autrement les niveaux sont « sympas », assez courts pour être rejoués itérativement jusqu’à les franchir, sans être vraiment frustré de mourir au dernier moment et devoir les relancer depuis le début, chacun apportant son ambiance et son panel d’ennemis uniques (et toujours super beaux :love:), les patterns sont classiques mais assez efficaces (sans être super stimulants non plus), et puis on a toute un tas de vaisseaux différents aux tirs variés et pour le coup assez intéressants à jouer (pas super équilibrés toutefois, certains ont des bonnes idées qui changent bien la façon de jouer, mais malheureusement pas super efficaces non plus tels que les dommages ont été définis … du coup on les abandonne vite … dommage).

Il y a très peu de niveaux, qui sont très courts, mais avant de les franchir avec l’obligation d’incrémenter progressivement la difficulté, il va falloir un peu de temps aux néophytes de ce genre de jeu dont je fais partie ; et le dernier niveau offre un mur soudain de difficulté qui me laisse sur ma faim (où les rideaux de boulettes se doublent de couloirs étroits dans lesquels il faut slalomer fébrilement pour ne pas se faire écraser par le scrolling forcé, plus frustrant que plaisant).

[b]Donc bref, c’est très joli, plutôt efficace (tout en restant très classique) sur ses fondamentaux, mais fait certains choix qui me semblent vraiment plus frustrants qu’amusants ou intéressants. Je pense que c’est à réserver aux amateurs du genre ascendance bullet hell, sinon, bof.[/b]

Jamestown+ é a versão mais nova e ampliada de Jamestown, pra quem não comprou ainda, ignore a versão anterior e se gostou da versão antiga, também compensa pois já vem as DLC's, novas fases, novas naves e um modo de jogo novo.

O jogo tem uma história ok, sobre a colônia de mesmo nome do jogo, que precisa se defender, é ignorável e tudo mais, mas é legal e tem artes bem legais na transição das fases.

A ideia é jogar cada fase, liberando naves e tudo mais, cada uma consiste em 2 continues e é bem tranquilo de forma geral, mas você conforme joga libera novas dificuldades que continuam a progredir na história. É uma ideia simples e bem executada.

Porém... ao terminar o jogo, você vai simplesmente continuar jogando porque o jogo é simplesmente bom, e vai te dar mais e mais formas de continuar jogando. Então ao terminar as fases, se libera o Gauntlet e o Super Gauntlet. É basicamente o modo arcade.

Gauntlet tem as fases do jogo padrão, e o Super tem as mesmas fases e o adicional das fases Phobos que são na lua, uma side story que incrementa parte da narrativa e tem chefes bem legais. Ou seja, um arcade de 5 e 7 fases. Simples assim.

O que pode (e provavelmente vai) incomodar é a dificuldade do jogo, que beira o surreal dependendo da dificuldade, deixando até mesmo de ser divertido, porque é meramente uma mistura de decorar TUDO que pode acontecer somado a uma boa dose de sorte. Principalmente se for tentar o 100%.

O sistema do jogo me prendeu muito, tem um multiplicador que gera um escudo e te deixa invulnerável por alguns segundos te permitindo respirar, e o mesmo vale pra quando você manualmente encerra o multiplicador, gerando um escudo menor e mais curto na duração. E tem pelo menos 10 naves diferentes e 2 que basicamente são naves random do jogo, gerando uma nova nave ao morrer e ao passar de fase.

A música é excelente, a jogabilidade é precisa, e uma coisa curiosa é o fato de usar a tela inteira ao invés de usar o padrão vertical, e eles sabendo disso já fizeram ajustes que contribuem pra jogatina, como inimigos e balas maiores, naves bem menos aceleradas e embora seja um bullet hell dependendo da dificuldade, não é uma coisa injusta e que prejudica a sua dinâmica de jogo.

E pra melhorar, ainda consiste em co-op local de até 4 jogadores. Sendo assim uma ótima forma de jogar um jogo divertido e bem feito com amigos.

Jamestown ao meu ver, está na elite dos shmups do Steam, sendo brevemente diferente sem perder a base do gênero, contribuindo muito pro co-op local, e uma jogabilidade excelente ao lado de músicas incríveis. Não é nenhum exagero ver ele em listas de melhores shmups de toda a plataforma.

Don't let my playtime fool you, I've sunken a lot of time into the original Jamestown. This game was my introduction to the world of Bullet Hell shooters, and it's glorious.

Set in an alternate history where space travel was accomplished in the early 1600s, you play as Raleigh (or one of his comrades), who has been sentenced to death for his crimes on Earth, and has thus travelled to the colonies of Mars, seeking to clear his name. This leads you onto an epic conquest across Mars, blasting hordes of Martians and Spanish War Machines, into an adventure to save Jamestown from the wrath of a destructive Conquistador.

The story is admittedly barebones - really, it's just an excuse for you to blow stuff up - but it ties the game together with a steampunk sci-fi theme that I absolutely love, so I'm not complaining.

You can play using keyboard, mouse, or controller. I used to play with mouse because I thought it felt "natural" to guide your ship through the storm of bullets with your cursor. In recent times, however, I find playing with the mouse to be a bit disorientating, because your ship doesn't travel at the same relative speed as your hand across the mousepad. That said, I do want to mention that you can plug in multiple mice for co-op play, and each mouse will control its own ship. I know that sounds like a no-brainer - hardly any different from a second player plugging in a second controller on a games console - but I just think it's amusing.

Gameplay is fairly simple. [Joystick/Directional Buttons/Pad/Move mouse] to move, [Button 1] to shoot, [Button 2] to fire your Special weapon, don't get shot, or you die. There are multiple ships you can choose from, and each one has their own unique weapons and playstyle. 

Here's a few of the ships you can mess around with:
[b]Beam[/b] is one of the two ships you start with. It shoots a fan of projectiles for its primary attack, but its special launches a powerful constant beam in front of you, which does a lot of damage, but slows you down while it's active. This ship is very straightforward, and is great for new players.
[b]Gunner[/b] fires two different laser cannons at once, but his special "attack" changes the orientation of one of them, allowing them to shoot in nearly any direction they want. This is one of the more technical ships available, but I can imagine god-tier player making VERY good use of it.
[b]Charge[/b] (my personal favourite) only shoots straight in front of it, but its special weapon launches a huge, slow-travelling ball of energy that phases through enemies (and walls), leaving a path of destruction in its wake. Unlike other ships that impair you while using/charging your special attack, the ball is launched instantly, and afterword, you can forget about it and focus on dodging bullets. This attack charges overtime, meaning if you try to rapid-fire it, it will launch smaller, less powerful energy balls. Compared to the Beam, it's crowd-control capabilities aren't as great, but it's amazing against larger enemies, especially bosses.
[b]Gunpowder[/b] is the other ship that you start with (originally, it was part of a DLC pack, but now said pack comes packaged with this version). It's similar to the Charge ship in that its special charges overtime, rather than when held. The ship will gradually produce powder kegs that will orbit you, and for some reason are also mounted with guns that fire whenever you do. This can give you a huge range of fire, in comparison to your puny hit box. If you need a burst of damage though, your special attack will launch one of your kegs forward, and it'll explode. I still prefer Charge, but I can't deny that Gunpowder is fun to mess around with.
There are several other ship types you can unlock (including some new, customizable ships that I haven't touched yet, but seem pretty cool), but I won't mention for the sake of time. I guarantee that you'll find one that you enjoy. Though if you're feeling indecisive or cocky, there is also the unlockable [b]Fortune[/b] ship, which is this game's version of the Random character select option.

Enough about ships, this is where the game gets more interesting: The [b]Vaunt[/b] system. 
Defeated enemies drop gold, which you can collect to charge your [b]Vaunt[/b] gauge. Once the gauge is fully charged, you can press [Button 3] to enter [b]Vaunt![/b] (Yes, I'm going to bold the word [b]Vaunt[/b] every time I type it, deal with it) This will grant you a temporary shield that blocks all bullets (and it's large enough that some friends could hide under it if they need a moment). [b]Vaunt[/b] will remain active for some time after the shield disappears, while your [b]Vaunt[/b] gauge slowly drains. During this time, your bullets will turn Mace-Windu-purple (this is clearly the most significant feature). Once [b]Vaunt[/b] expires, you'll gain a point bonus depending on how long your [b]Vaunt[/b] lasted. However, if you find yourself in a pickle, you can press [button 3] while [b]Vaunt[/b] is still active to bring up another shield, at the cost of ending [b]Vaunt[/b] early, and preventing the [b]Vaunt[/b] meter from charging up again for a few seconds. 
This system, if used effectively, can serve as a great Get-out-of-jail-free card, and [i]if you only want to beat the game, that's all you ever need to think of it as[/i]. But if you want to gun for a high score, you'll want to try and keep your [b]Vaunt[/b] going as long as possible, blasting enemies and collecting gold to keep the gauge charged, while forgoing protection and dodging attacks. I believe the old phrase is, "git gud".

I love this game - it's a great sci-fi romp, but it will chew you up and spit you out if you don't take it seriously. Which leads into my complaints...

Firstly, the campaign is short. Each level is only a few minutes long, and there are only 5 levels in the base game (the Plus version adds two more levels). Hypothetically, if you aced every level on your first try, you could clear the campaign in about an hour, maybe less. I consider this a good problem to have - better a short and fun experience than a long and boring one. If you're really desperate for more game though, there are a series of challenge levels you can play through that put your skills to the test.

However - second complaint - the last two levels (plus one of the bonus levels) are gated by difficulty. In order to unlock the final level, you must clear all the previous levels on Legendary difficulty or harder. If you've been playing on Normal or Difficult, this can feel like a kick to the face. I believe some may call this a method of "Padding" - artificially increasing playtime to make the game seem longer than it actually is. Though if you were to embrace the challenge and dive in at Legendary difficulty form the start, then this won't be an issue for you.

Oh yeah, I completely forgot to mention the game's soundtrack!
It's good. The orchestra nails the tone of every scene. A couple highlights for me include the build-up until you arrive at the lost colony of Roanoke (or what's left of it...), the theme of the New Madrid mining colony, and I would be remiss not to mention the theme that plays during the final fight against the Conquistador.
My favourite track, though, is the jingle that plays at the end of each level - it's a joyous jaunt that fills me with dopamine every time I hear it (as if the excitement from defeating the boss hadn't already topped it).

Overall...
If you have the original Jamestown already, buy the plus version when it's on sale. 
If you love bullet hell games, but have never played Jamestown, buy Jamestown+ and remedy this issue immediately.
If you haven't played bullet hell games before, but you're interested in the genre, this is a good place to start, but be prepared to face that difficulty gate.

A great shmup for fans of Cave's classic shoot 'em up titles and the wider genre, with a neat fantasy setting. This game does not let the player set the difficulty to easy and breeze through the whole experience, so know that going in. But also, know this. I am not very good at shmups, and I was able to complete the campaign and get the credits roll on Legendary. So it can be done without being a pro at these games.

While continues are limited, there is a level select screen, so you can replay specifically the area that's been giving you trouble, getting full credit for completing it at the selected difficulty, and progressing the story. And while the levels themselves, leading up to the boss, can be tricky later on, a little experience with them should have you reaching the boss with a continue left. Which was enough, even for me, because these fights are tough but fair.

Saving up your credits to spend on the Gunner ship might help, here. I found the starting ship to be my favorite until I unlocked the ability to buy the Gunner, but then the latter took over as my favorite. It has a beam weapon that fires along with your main armament, and can be aimed with the secondary attack button. But I found that just leaving it facing forward was ideal. It gave my ship a powerful, focused forward attack, without slowing it down or requiring any management of two attack buttons. So I could focus on dodging, eliminating threats, and timing my use of the "vaunt" button's shield ability.

Более того, последний уровень нельзя пройти на первых двух сложностях (а предпоследний нельзя пройти на самой первой). Отлично, не так ли? Два дополнительных уровня идут отдельно. Зачем разработчики так сделали? Ответ прост: растянуть время прохождения. Так можно все 7 уровней пройти за час и справедливо оформить рефанд. Но ввиду принуждения к повышению сложности приходится переигрывать уровни. Так почему же я всё равно советую игру?

Jamestown was on many seasoned shoot 'em up players list of introductory shooters.  I can see why.  The game offers baby steps into the genre.  While boasting and interesting retro-futurist look at colonial America.  And huge number of unlockables extras from playing and practicing the game.

Speaking of unlockables, I found it interesting that with all the ships available to me, my go to the introductory beam ship. I suppose you can take me out of Cave games, but you can't take the Cave game outta me.  I think that illustrates an interesting point about Jamestown+.  You have a bunch of ships to unlock and pick from, but they are different ways to play the game.  Not better ways.  

I like that Jamestown+ default is to play each mission individually.  Rather than back-to-back like most shooters beyond some STGs practice mode.  Sometimes I just want to play a single stage, but I also don't just want it to be 'practice'.  In Jamestown it feels like progression.  As it unlocks additional stages and yields money to buy unlockable ships or mission types.  Including playing the entire game back-to-back like a more traditional shooter.

The game play has a good pace to it, and the enemies and bullet patterns are well crafted.  The game is a vertizontal.  With being on the correct side of the screen at the right time key during the single player experience.  I suspect this is less the game during co-op.  The player is armed with standard array of weapons: regular shot, focus shot, consumable bombs and a recharging hyper.  

A slight annoyance is the re-mapping of the buttons each game.  However, as someone that uses on odd controller for shooters on Steam (8-button Sega Genesis), it's much better than many re-mapping schemes I've dealt with.  And that's just the games that allow me to use my controller of choice.

I hearty agree with those that suggest Jamestown+ as an introductory shooter.  The game is highly accessible.  It makes use of common genre mechanics.  And it has a steadily increasing difficulty curve to both allow the player to get comfortable with the game and see much of it while requiring some practice and effort to see it to the end.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Jamestown+ is a SHMUP that is worth your time if you like SHUMPs. It's short; you can beat all of the stages on the "recommended" difficulty in about 2 hours. But there are lots of extra modes if you want to unlock them via the in game shop. 

Don't bother with the original if it's still available.

[h1]----Summary[/h1]
JamesTown+ is a top down Shooter with pixel graphics. It has a somewhat tacked on feeling story, but the graphics remind me a lot of Metal Slug, which is good. Hold the left/right mouse buttons and go to town. Your hitbox is small.


[h1]----Positives[/h1]
[h3]Up to 4 people can play[/h3]
Local only, so your friends (if you have any) need to be in the same room as you. There will be some artificial difficulty in that regard for those of you who inevitably buy this game. But it is a good time. Use a mouse, keyboard, or controller.


[h3]Can use multiple mice[/h3]
While the mouse is the most causal way to play this, it must be said how impressive it is that each player can use their own mouse if they want.

The game doesn't register the middle button as being pressed on one of my wireless mice, but it is still very cool. I imagine it will also let you use multiple keyboards, which is also cool, and multiple controllers, which is less cool.

Still very cool.

[h3]Nice Graphics[/h3]
Pixel art looks nice, with great animations. I will say the in between graphics for the story have that "fake pixel art" look to them, but they are far from offensive. I give this a 88/100 Metal Slug pixels.

[h3]Music is good[/h3]
Has a slightly overproduced feel for some of the songs, but I think its good overall.

[h3]Nice Ship Variety[/h3]
While I don't like every ship, a few of them are interesting enough for me to prefer one over another depending on the stage.

[h1]----Negatives[/h1]
[h3]Cannot Rebind controls[/h3]
Had to use a different mouse than I usually use because apparently middle click on my mouse doesn't mean middle click on all mice. It would have been a lot better if I could bind it to the back/forward buttons I have on my mouse so I don't need to move my fingers off the fire button.

Key rebinding is pretty standard for most game engines these days, and the fact this was (re)released in 2019 says that you should have tried harder.

[h3]Poor ship balance[/h3]
I'm not a SHMUP pro, but some of these ships feel like they were included specifically for variety instead of being more useful for specific scenarios. While I'm sure you can do beat the game with every ship, some ships are way better than the others. I recommend the missile ship, the first one you get, and the one that lets you place the laser wherever you want.


[h3]Game Crashed[/h3]
The game crashed twice between levels. I still got the credit for beating those levels, but it was a bit annoying.


[h1]----Conclusion[/h1]
I had a good two hours with this. If more of the ships were fun, I would say I'd play more, but for now I think I'll revisit it on occasion. Dunno if it goes on sale, since I had this from a long time ago, I think from a humble bundle, but I would wait for a sale. 

Don't bother with the original if it's still available.

My initial experience with Jamestown was a bit rough. The greatest issue of the game is that most of its wide variety of ships are not viable for solo play on higher difficulties.
The wide aspect ratio for a vertically scrolling game puts most ships at a great disadvantage as they simply can not take out enough enemies before being overwhelmed and move too slowly.
However, there is one ship that is fun, fast and viable for everything in this game: The Treason ship.
Thanks to that ship, I have spent a lot of time during the last year grinding the highest difficulty and came to truly appreciate all the hard work put into Jamestown and Jamestown+.

A lot of detail is put into the stage design as each stage has a completely unique set of enemies and boss.
Some of these enemies are worth more points and drop more items if special requirements are fulfilled while destroying them.
The gorgeous art and music strongly contribute to all the flavor.

The game was designed around being played in co-op. It doesn't offer online play but if you get the chance to play locally with friends, you're in for a good time.
Co-op gameplay requires you to watch out for your allies. Either by protecting them with your Vaunt or collecting revival items to revive fallen players.
Enemies have more health depending on the player count and if you're the only player left, the stakes can get very high. It's a very fun dynamic.

The scoring system is simple but engaging: Maintain your Vaunt for as long as you can by continuously collecting items and fulfil the special requirements of enemies.
If you play co-op: Have every other member activate their Vaunt to increase the multiplier as your Vaunt runs out and cash in on a lot of score.
You can cancel a Vaunt manually for invincibility frames but it will half the Vaunt bonus.

CONTEXTE : je cherche des jeux PC exclusivement en mode CO-OP local, pour jouer avec mes 2 kids (7 et 9 ans) = coop local avec au moins 3 joueurs. Il faut donc que ça leur plaise et qu'on puisse y jouer (la jouabilité c'est plus moi qui suis limitée = suis mega nulle en jeux video, ma dernière "experience pixel" datant des feux jeux MSX...), et eux avec leurs copains, dans un ultime mouvement de resistance contre la "vague autistique Brawl Star" qui fait rage en ce moment...bref je cherche "du game, de la video avec de la convivialité tout dedans".

VERDICT : testé ce w-e avec mes kids + 1 de leur copain (9 ans. ça fait donc 4 joeurs), c'etait notre premiere fois (toute-toute) en mode Bullet Hell. evidemment c'est le bordel, ça clignote de partout, parfois tu sais mème plus ou es ton vaisseau, tu creves 9 ou 20 fois (j'ai dit qu'on etait novices, non ? ben voilà, mème en mode normal on a souffert). tu tires, tu retires, tu fais glisser ton vaisseau desesperement, t'essaies d'avoir les anneaux et de sauver tes zzzamis qui ont tous peri au champ d'honneur, avant de ne crever toi mème malgré cette fantastique esquive de la dernière chance... La musique est delicieusement ringarde (et non pas saoulante du tout), comme les graphismes du temps de mes premiers jeux videos (si tu veux un truc epuré et minimaliste, ben non, prends pas celui-là). 
y'a shop à l'interieur du jeu (never too late...), des fois que tu te demandes - comme nous - à quoi servent tous ces points : tu peux changer ton vaisseau/tes armes blablabla. 

DUREE DE VIE : bizarrement, c'est un jeu auquel tu reviens - mème si c'est toujours la mème chose - si t'as envie de te detendre, en mode je pose mon cerveau et je prends ma manette. et franchement c'est très rafraichissant. C'est facile, t'as pas de puzzle, pas de texte, juste un demi milliers de boules de couleurs pourtant très avenantes qui viennent sur toi quand toi tu veux pas d'elles.

donc oui, oui pour les kids et oui pour moi.
